chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's order. A compass keeps one distance fixed, so circles and arcs give exact lengths; squares and rectangles are then built from their properties, and the same two ideas, perpendiculars and arcs, find every corner.

points.title: Draw, then reason
points.text: Each construction starts from a rough diagram and a prediction, then the steps are carried out and checked with a ruler and a protractor.

points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: worked videos for the book's examples, one tool to do it by hand where the manipulation is the idea, then the book's construction questions in a practice topic.

points.title: Properties do the work
points.text: A square and a rectangle have fixed properties, so we measure only what is needed and the properties give the remaining sides and angles.

points.title: Keeko's doubts
points.text: Wrong ideas such as 'a square is not a rectangle' or 'a diagonal always splits a corner into two equal angles' are raised by Keeko and fixed with a drawing, never just a rule.

1. Make a guess before the next step: can you draw a perfect circle freehand, with no help at all? Try one on paper.
2. Now trace a bangle and put the two next to each other. The freehand one wobbles, the traced one is round.
3. A ruler draws straight lines and a compass draws round curves. With these two tools we can build faces, waves, houses, squares and rectangles exactly.

content.text:
1. Predict first: five pictures are all made of circles. Which one looks hardest to draw by hand, and why?
2. Two equal circles can touch, two circles can share one centre with the inner one smaller, and three equal circles can overlap in a row.
3. A mouse face is one big circle for the face and two smaller circles for the ears.
4. Freehand circles are uneven. We need a tool that keeps one distance fixed.

content.text:
Worked example: Look at five artwork pictures: two circles of the same size side by side and touching; two circles one inside the other with the same centre (the inner one about half the size of the outer); three equal circles in a row, each overlapping the next; a mouse face (one big circle for the face, two smaller circles for the ears, two small circles with dots for the eyes, a dot for the nose and a short line for the mouth); and two lines crossing like an X with a small circle at the bottom end of each line. Try drawing them freehand.
1. Look at each picture and spot the circles in it.
2. Sketch the circles in the right places and sizes.
3. Compare your freehand circles with the pictures and see how round they are.
Answer: Open ended. A correct drawing uses round circles of the sizes and positions described. Freehand circles are usually uneven, which is why a compass is introduced next.

1. Predict first: mark P and then every point that is exactly 4 cm from P. What shape will the dots make?
2. Put the 0 cm mark of the ruler on P, never the end of the ruler, and mark a point at 4 cm. Turn the ruler and mark another.
3. After many turns the dots make a round shape around P: a circle with centre P.

content.text:
Worked example: Mark a point P in your notebook. Then mark as many points as possible, in different directions, that are 4 cm away from P.
1. Mark P in the middle of the page.
2. Place the ruler with 0 cm at P and mark a point at 4 cm.
3. Turn the ruler to another direction and mark another point at 4 cm from P; repeat in many directions.
4. Notice the points form a round shape around P.
Answer: All the points you mark lie on a round curve around P, each exactly 4 cm from P. With enough points they join into a circle of radius 4 cm.

concepts.concept_name: All the points 4 cm from P

content.text:
Worked example: Imagine marking all the points that are 4 cm away from the point P. How would they look?
1. Every point is the same distance, 4 cm, from P.
2. Joining all such points gives a perfectly round curve.
3. This curve is a circle with centre P.
Answer: They would form a circle with centre P and radius 4 cm.

concepts.concept_name: The compass draws the circle: centre and radius

content.text:
You can start by marking a few points of distance 4 cm from P using the compass. How can this be done?
You will have to open up the compass against a ruler (see Fig. 8.2) such that the distance between the tip of the compass and the pencil is 4 cm.
Now, try to get the full curve.
Hint: Keep the point of the compass fixed moving only the pencil.
What is the shape of the curve? It is a circle!
Take a point on the circle. What will be its distance from P, equal to 4 cm, less than 4 cm or greater than 4 cm? Similarly, what will be the distance between P and another point on the circle?
As shown in the figure, the point P is called the centre of the circle and the distance between the centre and any point on the circle is called the radius of the circle.

content.text:
1. Predict first: with the tip fixed on P and the pencil swung around, is any point of the curve nearer to P than 4 cm?
2. Open the compass against a ruler until the tip and the pencil are 4 cm apart. Fix the tip at P and move only the pencil.
3. The pencil stays 4 cm from the tip all the way round. The fixed point is the centre and that fixed distance is the radius.
4. Keeko thinks the compass opening is the width of the whole circle. It is only the radius; the width is twice as much.

content.text:
Worked example: How can a compass be used to mark points that are 4 cm from P?
1. Place the compass next to a ruler and open it until the tip and the pencil point are 4 cm apart.
2. Put the tip firmly on P.
3. Keep the tip fixed and move only the pencil all the way round.
Answer: Open the compass so that the distance between its tip and the pencil is 4 cm (check against a ruler). Fix the tip at P and swing the pencil; every point it marks is 4 cm from P, giving a full circle.

concepts.concept_name: The compass draws the circle: centre and radius

content.text:
Worked example: Take a point on the circle drawn with centre P and radius 4 cm. Is its distance from P equal to 4 cm, less than 4 cm or greater than 4 cm? What about any other point on the circle?
1. The pencil stayed exactly 4 cm from the tip all the time.
2. So every point on the circle is 4 cm from P.
3. This fixed distance is the radius; P is the centre.
Answer: Equal to 4 cm for every point on the circle. P is called the centre and the distance from the centre to any point on the circle is called the radius.

content.text:
A circle is all the points at one fixed distance from the centre.
Set the compass opening against a ruler before drawing, and keep the tip fixed.
Touching circles have centres two radii apart; concentric circles share a centre.

concepts.concept_name: Activity (section 8.1)

content.text:
Activity (section 8.1): Using a ruler and a compass, recreate the artwork pictures: two touching circles, two circles with the same centre, three overlapping circles, the mouse face, and the X with two small circles. Try to make them look as good as the book's pictures.
1. Choose a radius and set the compass with the ruler.
2. Fix the tip at each centre and draw each circle.
3. For concentric circles, keep the same tip point and change the radius.
4. Add the dots and lines with a ruler.
Answer: Open ended. Correct drawings: touching circles have centres at a distance of twice the radius; concentric circles share one centre but have different radii; overlapping circles have centres closer than twice the radius; the mouse face has all its circles drawn with a compass.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a line AB is 8 cm long and two equal half circles share it, one above the line and one below. How long is the flat side of each half circle?
2. The two flat sides split AB into two equal parts of 4 cm each. Each flat side is the diameter of its half circle.
3. The radius is half of the diameter, so the radius is 2 cm. The tip goes at the middle of each flat side, 2 cm from the end.

content.text:
Worked example: Construct this wave: a central straight line AB = 8 cm. The first wave is a half circle on the left half of AB lying above the line (A to X), and the second wave is a half circle on the right half lying below the line (X to B). Both half circles are shaded with vertical lines.
1. Draw AB = 8 cm with a ruler.
2. Mark X on AB at 4 cm from A.
3. Set the compass to 2 cm; put the tip at the point 2 cm from A and draw a half circle above AB from A to X.
4. Put the tip at the point 6 cm from A (2 cm from B) and draw a half circle below AB from X to B.
5. Shade both half circles with vertical lines.
Answer: AB = 8 cm, AX = XB = 4 cm. Each half circle has diameter 4 cm, so radius 2 cm. First half circle: tip at the point 2 cm from A on AB, drawn above the line. Second half circle: tip at the point 6 cm from A on AB, drawn below the line.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q1 (section 8.1): In the wave with a central line AB = 8 cm, the first wave is a half circle from A to X on the line AB. What radius should be taken in the compass to get this half circle? What should be the length of AX? a) What radius should be taken in the compass? b) What should be the length of AX?
1. The two equal half circles share the 8 cm line, so AX is 8 cm divided by 2, which gives 4 cm.
2. AX is the diameter of the half circle.
3. Radius = 4 cm ÷ 2 = 2 cm.
Answer: a) 2 cm, b) AX = 4 cm

content.text:
Figure it Out Q2 (section 8.1): Take a central line of a different length and try to draw the wave on it.
1. Draw a line AB of any length L.
2. Mark the middle point X.
3. Set the compass to L ÷ 4 and draw the first half circle above AB from A to X.
4. Draw the second half circle below AB from X to B with the same radius.
Answer: Open ended. For a central line of length L, each half circle has diameter L ÷ 2 and radius L ÷ 4. Example: L = 10 cm gives two half circles of diameter 5 cm and radius 2.5 cm; L = 12 cm gives radius 3 cm.

content.text: 1. A Person: How will you draw this? This figure has two components. You might have figured out a way of drawing the first part. For drawing the second part, see this. content.text:
1. Predict first: the top of the body dips in the middle like a smile. Does the compass tip go on the body, or somewhere above it?
2. The head is a circle with centre in the middle above the neck. The body top is an arc, and the tip of the compass is above the body, in line with the middle.
3. Fix a radius, try a tip point above the body, and check that the arc passes through both top corners and touches the neck.

content.text:
Worked example: Draw a person made of a circle for the head, a short straight neck line below it, and a body that is a rectangle whose top edge is a curved arc dipping in the middle. How will you draw the curved top of the body with a compass? Where should the tip be placed and what radius should be used?
1. Draw the head circle with the compass.
2. Draw the neck as a short vertical line below the circle.
3. Draw the body as a rectangle without the top edge: two vertical sides and a flat bottom.
4. Fix a radius and try the tip at different spots above the body until the arc from one top corner to the other touches the bottom of the neck line.
5. Draw the arc and rub out the trial marks.
Answer: Open ended. The head is a circle. The body is a rectangle with vertical sides and a flat bottom, and its top is an arc of a circle joining the two top corners and dipping down in the middle. The compass tip goes above the body (outside it, on the line through the middle of the body) at a point found by trial, and the radius is the distance from that tip to the top corners. The neck line joins the bottom of the head to the lowest point of the arc.

content.text:
1. Predict first: an eye is two curves meeting at two pointed ends. Do both curves use the same radius?
2. Draw two light guide lines. The tip of the upper curve is on one line and the tip of the lower curve is on the other.
3. Keep the same radius and the same distance from the middle for both tips. Then the eye is symmetrical, and the second eye is a copy of the first.

content.text:
Worked example: How do you draw these eyes with a compass? Each eye is an almond shape made of an upper curve and a lower curve meeting at two pointed corners, with a filled dark circle (pupil) in the middle. The two eyes sit side by side and are identical.
1. Draw two light horizontal guide lines (supporting lines) that help to place the compass tips.
2. Choose a radius and place the tip at B to draw the upper curve between the two corners.
3. Place the tip at A, the same distance from the middle on the other side, and with the same radius draw the lower curve.
4. Fill the pupil circle in the middle.
5. Repeat for the second eye and adjust until both eyes are symmetrical and identical.
Answer: Open ended. The upper and lower curves are arcs of equal radius. Their compass tips (points A and B) lie on the line through the middle of the eye, one on each side, equally far from the middle, so that the eye is symmetrical. Draw a filled circle in the middle as the pupil.

maths_rules: Head: a full circle drawn with the compass. Neck: a short straight line below the head.
Body: two vertical sides and a flat bottom; the two top corners are 6 cm apart, so each is 6 / 2 = 3 cm from the middle line.
The top edge is an arc of a circle joining the two top corners and dipping in the middle.
Tip on the middle line, 4 cm above the line joining the top corners; each top corner is then 5 cm from the tip (3-4-5 right triangle, checked with a ruler).
The lowest spot of the arc is 5 cm below the tip, which is 5 - 4 = 1 cm below the top corners.
Slip: a tip inside the body gives an arc that bulges upward, not one that dips.

source_video_walkthrough.title: How do two arcs make an eye with a compass?
items: How do you draw these eyes with a compass? Each eye is an almond shape made of an upper curve and a lower curve meeting at two pointed corners, with a filled dark circle (pupil) in the middle. The two eyes sit side by side and are identical.
source_video_walkthrough.intent: The child uses the arc idea of the person to draw two identical arcs, one with the tip below and one with the tip above.

interaction_points.prompt: How do you draw one eye with a compass?
interaction_points.answer: open ended; both arcs have equal radius, the tips lie on the line through the middle of the eye, one on each side, equally far from the middle (for an eye 6 cm wide: tips 4 cm from the middle line, opening 5 cm)
covers: How do you draw these eyes with a compass? Each eye is an almond shape made of an upper curve and a lower curve meeting at two pointed corners, with a filled dark circle (pupil) in the middle. The two eyes sit side by side and are identical.

source: How do you draw these eyes with a compass? Each eye is an almond shape made of an upper curve and a lower curve meeting at two pointed corners, with a filled dark circle (pupil) in the middle. The two eyes sit side by side and are identical.
video_script.why: The child uses the arc idea of the person to draw two identical arcs, one with the tip below and one with the tip above.
video_script.substitution: An eye six centimetres wide, with tips four centimetres from the middle line and an opening of five centimetres.
video_script.anchor: An almond eye made of an upper arc and a lower arc, with a dark pupil
video_script.wrong_answer: put the tip above the eye
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko wants to put the tip above the eye for the upper arc. A tip above makes the arc bulge downward like a bowl, but the upper arc must bulge upward, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: Both arcs use one opening, and the two tips sit equally far from the middle.

final_answer.value: open ended; both arcs have equal radius, the tips lie on the line through the middle of the eye, one on each side, equally far from the middle (for an eye 6 cm wide: tips 4 cm from the middle line, opening 5 cm)
final_answer.spoken: both arcs use one opening, and the two tips sit equally far from the middle; for an eye six centimetres wide the opening is five centimetres and each tip is four centimetres from the middle line

never_show: the finished eye before the answer
maths_rules: Each curve of the eye is an arc, a part of a circle.
The corners are on the middle line, 6 cm apart, so each is 6 / 2 = 3 cm from the centre of the eye.
Upper arc: tip 4 cm below the middle line, opening 5 cm; each corner is 5 cm from the tip (3-4-5 right triangle, checked with a ruler); the arc rises 5 - 4 = 1 cm above the middle line.
Lower arc: tip 4 cm above the middle line, the same opening 5 cm; the arc falls 1 cm below the middle line.
Same opening and equal distance from the middle give two identical arcs, so the eye is symmetrical and 1 + 1 = 2 cm tall.
Slip: a tip above the eye makes the arc bulge downward, not upward.
video_script.design: One idea: the upper arc has its tip below, the lower arc has its tip above, with one opening. Uses the arc idea of the person. Wrong idea: the tip goes on the same side as the arc. The eye stays all video.

content.text:
Figure it Out Q3, Try This (section 8.1): Try to recreate the figure where the waves are smaller than a half circle (as appearing in the neck of the figure 'A Person'). The challenge here is to get both the waves to be identical. This may be tricky!
1. Draw the central line and mark the chord for each wave.
2. Choose one radius bigger than half the chord.
3. For the upper arc, place the tip below the line on the perpendicular through the middle of the chord, at a fixed distance, and draw the arc above the line.
4. For the lower arc, place the tip above the line at the same distance from the line and use the same radius.
5. Check that both arcs look identical.
Answer: Open ended. Both waves are arcs of the same radius on the same length of chord. A correct drawing shows two identical arcs, one above the line and one below the line, each shorter than a half circle.

concepts.concept_name: The two properties of a rectangle and of a square

content.text:
Now, let us look at some basic figures having straight lines in their boundary.
What shapes are these? Yes, these are our familiar squares and rectangles. But what makes them squares and rectangles?
Consider this rectangle ABCD.
The points A, B, C and D are the corners of the rectangle. Lines AB, BC, CD and DA are its sides. Its angles are ∠A, ∠B, ∠C and ∠D.
The blue sides AB and CD are called opposite sides, as they lie opposite to each other. Likewise, AD and BC is the other pair of opposite sides.
Recall that, in a rectangle:
R1) The opposite sides are equal in length, and
R2) All the angles are 90°.
As in the case of rectangles, the corners and sides are defined for a square in the same manner.
A square satisfies the following two properties:
S1) All the sides are equal, and

concepts.concept_name: Naming a figure by its corners in order

content.text:
See the rectangle in Fig. 8.4 and the name given to it: ABCD. This rectangle can also be named in other ways, BCDA, CDAB, DABC, ADCB, DCBA, CBAD and BADC. So, can a rectangle be named using any combination of the labels around its corners? No! For example, it cannot be named ABDC or ACBD. Can you see what names are allowed and what names are not?
In a valid name, the corners occur in an order of travel around the rectangle, starting from any corner.

content.text:
Worked example: Which of the following is not a name for this square? The square has corners S (top left), P (top right), Q (bottom right) and R (bottom left). 1. PQSR 2. SPQR 3. RSPQ 4. QRSP 1) PQSR 2) SPQR 3) RSPQ 4) QRSP

3. PQSR goes from Q to S, which is a diagonal, so it is not a valid name.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q2 (section 8.2)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q2 (section 8.2): Identify if there are any squares in this collection. Use measurements if needed. On a dot grid there are four tilted 4-sided figures with corners on dots: A is a diamond whose left to right span equals its top to bottom span (about 8 dots each way); B is a diamond about 6 dots wide and 8 dots tall; C is a diamond about 10 dots wide and 8 dots tall; D is a small tilted long rectangle.
1. A square needs 4 equal sides and 4 angles of 90°.
2. A has equal width and height, so its sides and angles are equal: a square.
3. B and C have unequal widths and heights, so they are diamonds whose angles are not 90°.
4. D has two long and two short sides, so it is a rectangle, not a square.
Answer: A is a square.

concepts.concept_name: A rotated square is still a square

content.text:
Here is a square piece of paper having all its sides equal in length and all angles equal to 90°. It is rotated as shown in the figure. Is it still a square?
Let us check if the rotated paper still satisfies the properties of a square.
Are all the sides still equal? Yes.
Are all the angles still 90°? Yes.
Rotating a square does not change its lengths and angles.
Therefore, this rotated figure satisfies both the properties of a square and so, it is a square.
By the same reasoning, a rotated rectangle is still a rectangle.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a tilted figure has its corners on dots. Can you tell that its sides are equal without a ruler?
2. Go from one corner to the next by a number of dots across and a number down. If every side uses the same two numbers, the sides are equal.
3. At the next corner swap the two numbers: across becomes down. That is a turn of 90°.
4. So the dot positions alone show equal sides and right angles.

content.text:
Worked example: Is it possible to reason out if the sides are equal or not, and if the angles are right or not, without using any measuring instruments in the above figure? Can we do this by only looking at the position of corners in the dot grid?
1. Count how many dots across and how many down it takes to go from one corner to the next.
2. If every side uses the same counts, the sides are equal.
3. If the next side uses the counts swapped for a turn (across and down exchanged), the angle is 90°.
Answer: Yes. The positions of the dots make it possible. Moving from one corner to the next by the same number of dots across and down, and turning with the counts swapped, gives equal sides and right angles.

maths_rules: Take P at the top. The corner Q is 3 dots right and 2 dots down from P. The corner R is 2 dots left and 3 dots down from Q. The corner S is 3 dots left and 2 dots up from R. Then P is 2 dots right and 3 dots up from S.
Every side uses the counts 3 and 2, so every side has the same length (the square of that length is 3 x 3 + 2 x 2 = 9 + 4 = 13 square dot steps, but the video only compares the counts).
P to Q is 3 across and 2 down; turning this step by a quarter turn (90 degrees) swaps the counts: Q to R is 2 across and 3 down.
At every corner the next step is the previous step turned a quarter turn, so every angle is 90 degrees.
A rotation keeps lengths, so each turned step is as long as the one before it.

Colour-blind-safe colours: #009E73 for a positive/first idea, #D55E00 for a negative/contrasting idea, #0072B2 for a first set or step, #E69F00 for a second set or step, #CC79A7 for the focus or highlight, #6B7280 for construction lines and for anything struck out. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Keep it uncluttered: one main idea only, at most three objects or groups, generous white space around everything, large readable labels, nothing decorative. A tilted square on a dot grid, with two sides showing staircases, wide margins.

Exact structure: A grid of dots. A tilted square with corners P, Q, R, S on dots: P at (0, 0), Q at (3, −2), R at (5, 1), S at (2, 3). Side PQ is 3 across and 2 down, shown as a staircase in teal #0072B2. Side QR is 2 across and 3 down, shown as a staircase in amber #E69F00. The other 2 sides are plain lines. A small right-angle sign at Q. Exactly 4 corners.

Visible text, exactly and only: P; Q; R; 3 across, 2 down; 2 across, 3 down

Takeaway: Equal dot counts mean equal sides, and swapped counts mean a right angle.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q1 (section 8.2)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q1 (section 8.2): Draw the rectangle and four squares configuration (a rectangle in the middle, about twice as wide as tall, with four equal small squares placed near its four corners, one outside each corner, not touching it) on a dot paper. What did you do to recreate this figure so that the four squares are placed symmetrically around the rectangle? Discuss with your classmates.
1. Draw the rectangle on dots, counting dots along each side.
2. From each corner of the rectangle, move one dot diagonally outwards (same count each time).
3. Draw an equal square at each of the four places, counting the same number of dots for every square.
4. Use the same counts on the left and right, top and bottom so the figure is symmetrical.
Answer: Open ended. A correct drawing shows a rectangle with four equal squares around it placed in the same way at each corner. Book hint: draw the rectangle and then leave one dot distance diagonally to place the four smaller squares.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out Q3 (section 8.2)

content.text:
Figure it Out Q3 (section 8.2): Draw at least 3 rotated squares and rectangles on a dot grid. Draw them such that their corners are on the dots. Verify if the squares and rectangles that you have drawn satisfy their respective properties.
1. Pick dots as corners so that each side goes the same number of dots across and down for a square.
2. Join the corners with a ruler.
3. Measure the sides with the ruler.
4. Check the angles with a protractor or a set square.
Answer: Open ended. A correct drawing: each rotated square has 4 equal sides and 4 angles of 90°; each rotated rectangle has equal opposite sides and 4 angles of 90°. For example a diamond with corners 4 dots up, 4 dots right, 4 dots down and 4 dots left of its centre is a square.

maths_rules: Square 1: centre O, corners 4 dots up, 4 right, 4 down and 4 left of O. Each side goes 4 across and 4 down or up, so the 4 sides are equal; the sides turn through a quarter turn, so each angle is 90 degrees.

Square 2: P at (0, 0), Q at (3, 1), R at (2, 4), S at (-1, 3). The steps are 3 right 1 up, 1 left 3 up, 3 left 1 down, 1 right 3 down. Every side uses the counts 3 and 1, and each step is the previous one turned a quarter turn, so it is a square.

Rectangle: P at (0, 0), Q at (2, 2), R at (-1, 5), S at (-3, 3). The steps are 2 right 2 up, 3 left 3 up, 2 left 2 down, 3 right 3 down. Opposite sides use the same counts, so they are equal; the two kinds of step point along the two diagonals of the grid squares, at 90 degrees; the sides are not all equal, so it is a rectangle and not a square.
Check with a ruler for the sides and the corner of a book for the angles.

Worked example: How would you construct a square with a side of 6 cm? A square PQRS of side length 6 cm is constructed.
1. Draw PQ = 6 cm with a ruler.
2. Place the protractor with its centre at P and its baseline along PQ, mark 90° and draw a perpendicular through P.
3. Mark S on this perpendicular so that PS = 6 cm (ruler), or open the compass to 6 cm, tip at P, and mark an arc.
4. At Q draw the perpendicular to PQ and mark R with QR = 6 cm (with the compass: keep the radius at 6 cm and put the tip at Q).
5. Join R and S. Check RS = 6 cm, ∠R = 90°, ∠S = 90°.
Answer: Square PQRS with PQ = QR = RS = SP = 6 cm and all angles 90°. RS = 6 cm and ∠R = ∠S = 90°.

tool_config.idea: A square or a rectangle is built in order: one side, perpendiculars at both ends, the other corners at the right length, then the last side; the properties fix the lengths and angles that are not measured.
tool_config.screen: A drawing sheet with a ruler, a protractor and a compass; a list of steps that unlock one at a time; a measuring read-out for every side and angle; a Check button.
student_does: Predict the length of the fourth side before drawing it.
Choose the right tool for each step and carry it out.
Press Check and read the sides and angles.
challenges: A square of side 5 cm: how long is the fourth side? (5 cm)

concepts.concept_name: Four right angles force equal opposite sides

content.text: 3. Is it possible to construct a 4-sided figure in which all the angles are equal to 90° but opposite sides are not equal? (Try This)
content.publication_text: 3. Is it possible to construct a 4-sided figure in which all the angles are equal to 90° but opposite sides are not equal? (Try This)
lines: 3. Is it possible to construct a 4-sided figure in which all the angles are equal to 90° but opposite sides are not equal? (Try This)

content.text:
1. Predict first: can you draw a four-sided figure with all four angles 90° but opposite sides unequal?
2. Draw one side. The perpendiculars at its two ends never come closer or move apart, so they stay the same distance apart.
3. That makes the opposite side as long as the first side. So the opposite sides are always equal.
4. A four-sided figure with all angles 90° is therefore a rectangle.

steps: Predict first: can you draw a four-sided figure with all four angles 90° but opposite sides unequal?
Draw one side. The perpendiculars at its two ends never come closer or move apart, so they stay the same distance apart.
That makes the opposite side as long as the first side. So the opposite sides are always equal.
A four-sided figure with all angles 90° is therefore a rectangle.

content.text:
Worked example: Is it possible to construct a 4-sided figure in which all the angles are equal to 90° but opposite sides are not equal?
1. Draw one side and the two perpendiculars at its ends.
2. The two perpendiculars stay the same distance apart, so the opposite side is the same length as the first side.
3. So opposite sides are always equal.
Answer: No. If all four angles are 90° the figure is a rectangle, so its opposite sides are equal.

concepts.concept_name: Setting up the rectangle and guessing

content.text:
Construct a rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm.
Imagine X to be a point that can be moved anywhere along the side AD. Similarly, imagine Y to be a point that can be moved anywhere along the side BC. Note that X can also be placed on the end point A or D. Similarly, Y can also be placed on the end point B or C.
At which positions will the points X and Y be at their closest? When do you think they will be the farthest? What does your intuition say? Discuss with your classmates. (Math Talk)
Now, verify your guesses by placing the points X and Y on the sides and measure how near or far they are.
The distance between X and Y can be obtained by measuring the length of the line XY.
How does the minimum distance between the points X and Y compare to the length of AB?

concepts.concept_name: Setting up the rectangle and guessing

content.text:
Worked example: In rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm, X moves along side AD and Y moves along side BC. At which positions will the points X and Y be at their closest? When do you think they will be the farthest? What does your intuition say? Discuss with your classmates.
1. Try several positions with a ruler.
2. XY is 7 cm whenever X and Y are at equal distances from A and B.
3. XY is longest when X and Y are at opposite corners.
Answer: Closest: when X and Y are the same distance from A and B respectively (for example X = A and Y = B), where XY = 7 cm. Farthest: when X is at one corner and Y at the opposite corner (X = A and Y = C, or X = D and Y = B), where XY is a diagonal of about 8 cm 1 mm (√65 cm).

content.text:

2. You get 7 cm each time, which is the length of AB.
Answer: The minimum distance of XY is 7 cm, which is equal to AB.

content.text:
Change the positions of X and Y to check if there are other positions where they are at their nearest or farthest. You could construct multiple copies of the rectangle and try out various positions of X and Y.
How will you keep track of the lengths XY for different positions of X and Y?
Here is one way of doing it. Suppose here are some of the positions of X and Y that you have considered:
When X is 5 mm away from A and Y is 3 cm away from B, XY = ___ cm ___ mm.
When X is 1 cm away from A and Y is 1 cm away from B, XY = ___ cm ___ mm.
When X is 2 cm away from A and Y is 4 cm away from B, XY = ___ cm ___ mm and so on.
Is there a shorthand way of writing it down? In all the sentences, only the position of X, Y and the length XY changes. So we could write this as: (table: Distance of X from A, Distance of Y from B, Length of XY)

content.text:
Worked example: Rectangle ABCD has AB = 7 cm, BC = 4 cm. Measure XY and fill in: When X is 5 mm away from A and Y is 3 cm away from B, XY = __ cm __ mm. When X is 1 cm away from A and Y is 1 cm away from B, XY = __ cm __ mm. When X is 2 cm away from A and Y is 4 cm away from B, XY = __ cm __ mm. a) X is 5 mm from A and Y is 3 cm from B b) X is 1 cm from A and Y is 1 cm from B c) X is 2 cm from A and Y is 4 cm from B
1. Across the rectangle the distance is 7 cm; the up and down difference between the two points changes.
2. a) the difference is 3 cm − 5 mm = 2.5 cm, XY = √(49 + 6.25) ≈ 7.4 cm.
3. b) the difference is 0, XY = 7 cm.
4. c) the difference is 4 cm − 2 cm = 2 cm, XY = √(49 + 4) ≈ 7.3 cm.
Answer: a) 7 cm 4 mm, b) 7 cm 0 mm, c) 7 cm 3 mm

content.text:

content.text:
1. Predict first: if X and Y are the same distance from A and B, what shape is ABYX?
2. X and Y are at the same height, so XY runs straight across. All four angles of ABYX are 90° and opposite sides are equal, so ABYX is a rectangle and XY equals AB.
3. The farthest apart are opposite corners: X at A and Y at C, or X at D and Y at B.
4. Then XY is a diagonal, AC or BD, about 8.1 cm for this rectangle.

concepts.concept_name: A rectangle of two identical squares

content.text:
Explore: What about constructing a rectangle that can be divided into two identical squares? Can you try it?
It is wise to first plan and then construct. But how do we plan? Can you think of a way?
One way is to visualise the final figure by drawing a rough diagram of it.
What can we infer from this figure? Can you identify the equal sides? Since the two squares are identical, AB = BC and FE = ED. Since ABEF and BCDE are squares, all the sides in each of the squares are equal. This is written as: AF = AB = BE = FE; BE = BC = CD = ED. So, all the shorter lines are equal!
A convention is followed to represent equal sides. It is done by putting a '|' on the line. Refer to the rough figure.
Using this analysis, can you try constructing it? Remember, all that was asked for is a rectangle that can be divided into two identical squares and with no measurements imposed.
To draw the rectangle ACDF, one could assign any length to AF. For example, if we assign AF = 4 cm, then what must the length of AC be?
Explore: Can the rectangle now be completed?

content.text:
1. Predict first: if the shorter side AF is 4 cm, how long must AC be so the rectangle holds two identical squares?
2. Plan with a rough diagram. The two squares are identical, so AB = BC and AF = AB, and tick marks show equal sides.
3. AC is two squares side by side: 4 cm and 4 cm give 8 cm.
4. Draw AF, a perpendicular at A, and cut it with the compass at 4 cm twice.

content.text:
Worked example: Construct a rectangle ACDF that can be divided into two identical squares ABEF and BCDE, with no measurements imposed. If AF is assigned 4 cm, what must the length of AC be?
1. Draw a rough diagram: AB = BC and FE = ED, and all the short lines are equal (AF = AB = BE = FE = BC = CD = ED).
2. Draw AF = 4 cm.
3. Draw a line perpendicular to AF at A. With the compass tip at A and radius AF, mark B on this line.
4. Keep the same radius and mark C beyond B so that BC = AF.
5. Do the same at F to place the other corners and complete the rectangle ACDF.
Answer: AC = 8 cm. The rectangle is 8 cm by 4 cm.

concepts.concept_name: A rectangle of three identical squares

content.text:
Construct a rectangle that can be divided into 3 identical squares as shown in the figure.
Solution: If this seems difficult, let us simplify the problem.
In fact, one could proceed by drawing AF without even measuring its length using a ruler. We could then construct a line perpendicular to AF that is long enough to contain the other side. As AB = AF, we need to somehow transfer the length of AF to get the point B. How do we do it without a ruler? Can it be done using a compass? Observe how the length of AF is measured using a compass. Use it to mark out the points B and C, and complete the rectangle.
With this idea, try constructing a rectangle that can be divided into three identical squares.

content.text:
Worked example: Construct a rectangle that can be divided into 3 identical squares (a rectangle split by two vertical lines into three equal squares).
1. Choose the square side, say 3 cm.
2. Draw a rough diagram showing 3 equal squares side by side.
3. Draw AB = 3 cm, draw perpendiculars at A and B, and mark AD = 3 cm and BC = 3 cm.
4. Use the compass to transfer the 3 cm length along the line two more times so that the total length is 9 cm.
5. Draw the dividing lines to check each part is a 3 cm square.
Answer: Any rectangle whose length is 3 times its breadth, for example 9 cm by 3 cm. Each square has side 3 cm.

content.text:
1. Predict first: can a rectangle 4 cm by 2.5 cm be cut into two identical squares?
2. Two identical squares need the length to be 2 times the breadth. Here 2 times 2.5 cm is 5 cm, not 4 cm.
3. Three identical squares need the length to be 3 times the breadth. A rectangle 7 cm by 2 cm fails, because 3 times 2 cm is 6 cm.
4. Many answers are possible, so test any pair with the length-to-breadth rule.

Worked example: Give the lengths of the sides of a rectangle that cannot be divided into two identical squares, and of a rectangle that cannot be divided into three identical squares. a) Cannot be divided into two identical squares b) Cannot be divided into three identical squares
1. A rectangle splits into two identical squares only if length = 2 × breadth.
2. 4 cm is not 2 × 2.5 cm.
3. It splits into three only if length = 3 × breadth; 7 cm is not 3 × 2 cm.
Answer: a) for example 4 cm by 2.5 cm, b) for example 7 cm by 2 cm (other answers possible)

concepts.concept_name: Construct 1: A Square within a Rectangle (section 8.4)

content.text:
Construct 1: A Square within a Rectangle (section 8.4): Construct a rectangle of sides 8 cm and 4 cm. How will you construct a square inside, as shown in the figure, such that the centre of the square is the same as the centre of the rectangle? (The square touches the top and bottom of the rectangle and sits in the middle of its length.)
1. Draw the 8 cm by 4 cm rectangle.
2. The square must fit between top and bottom, so its side is 4 cm.
3. Leave (8 cm − 4 cm) ÷ 2 = 2 cm on each side.
4. Mark points 2 cm in from each short side and draw the vertical lines of the square.
Answer: The square has side 4 cm. Its left and right sides are 2 cm away from the left and right sides of the rectangle.

3. Put the tip there and draw a circle inside the square. The hole is centred.

Construct 6: Square with Curves, Try This (section 8.4): This is a square with 8 cm sidelengths. Construct it so that four arcs, one on each side, bulge uniformly inwards from each side, each arc going from one corner of its side to the other corner.
1. Draw a square of side 8 cm.
2. Open the compass to 8 cm.
3. Put the tip at one end of a side and mark an arc outside the square; do the same from the other end; the two arcs cross at a point outside.
4. Put the tip at that crossing point and draw the arc from one corner to the other.
5. Repeat for the other three sides.
Answer: Open ended. A correct drawing: a square of side 8 cm with four equal arcs bulging inward. For example, use radius 8 cm and place each compass tip outside the square at the point that is 8 cm from both ends of that side; each arc then dips about 1 cm into the square.

content.text:
Consider a rectangle PQRS. Join PR and QS. These two lines are called the diagonals of the rectangle.
Compare the lengths of the diagonals. First predict the answer. Then construct a rectangle marking the points as shown and measure the diagonals.

concepts.concept_name: How a diagonal splits the corners

content.text:
In rectangle PQRS, the right angles at P and R are referred to as opposite angles. The other pair of opposite angles are the right angles at Q and S.
Observe that a diagonal divides each of the pair of opposite angles into two smaller angles. In the figure, the diagonal PR divides angle R into two smaller angles which we simply call g and h. The diagonal also divides angle P into c and d. Are g and h equal? Are c and d equal?
First predict the answers, and then measure the angles. What do you observe? Identify pairs of angles that are equal.

content.text:
Worked example: In rectangle PQRS the diagonal PR divides angle R into g and h, and divides angle P into c and d. Predict, then measure: are g and h equal? Are c and d equal? a) Are g and h equal? b) Are c and d equal?
1. Draw a rectangle that is not a square, for example 6 cm by 4 cm, and its diagonal PR.
2. Measure c, d at P and g, h at R with a protractor.
3. For 6 cm by 4 cm the angles are about 34° and 56°, so c and d differ.
4. In a square both angles are 45°.
5. In each case the two small angles add up to 90°.
Answer: a) g and h are not equal unless the rectangle is a square; b) c and d are not equal unless the rectangle is a square. In every rectangle g + h = 90° and c + d = 90°.

concepts.concept_name: How a diagonal splits the corners

content.text:
Worked example: In rectangle PQRS, with both diagonals drawn, the eight angles formed by the diagonals and the sides are a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h (at P: c and d; at Q: e and f; at R: g and h; at S: a and b; c is next to side PS, d next to PQ, e next to QP, f next to QR, g next to RQ, h next to RS, a next to SR, b next to SP). Measure them. Which angles are equal?
1. Draw a rectangle that is not a square and both its diagonals.
2. Measure all eight angles with a protractor.
3. The four angles next to the long sides come out equal: d, e, a, h.
4. The four angles next to the short sides come out equal: c, f, g, b.
5. Each pair from the two groups adds up to 90°.
Answer: d = e = a = h (the four angles next to the sides PQ and SR) and c = f = g = b (the four angles next to the sides PS and QR). Also c + d = 90°.

content.text:
1. Predict first: how should the sides of a rectangle be chosen so that the diagonal splits the corner into two equal angles?
2. Keep one side 4 cm and change the other: 5 cm, 6 cm, 4.5 cm. The two angles stay unequal.
3. Only when the two sides are equal, 4 cm and 4 cm, do both angles come out 45°.

content.text:
Worked example: How should the rectangle be constructed so that the diagonal divides the opposite angles into equal parts?
1. Try rectangles whose sides are different: the diagonal splits the right angle into unequal parts.
2. Make the adjacent sides equal, for example 5 cm and 5 cm.
3. Draw the diagonal and measure: both parts are 45°.
4. So only a square works.
Answer: The two adjacent sides must be equal, that is, the rectangle must be a square. Then each diagonal divides the opposite angles into 45° and 45°.

content.text:
Worked example: In your experiment, consider the case when all four sides of the rectangle are equal, that is, a square. Draw a square (for example with side 5 cm), draw both diagonals, and see what happens.
1. Draw a square of side 5 cm.
2. Join both diagonals.
3. Measure the eight angles with a protractor: each is 45°.
4. Measure the diagonals: both are about 7.1 cm.
Answer: In a square each diagonal divides the opposite angles into 45° and 45°. All eight angles formed by the diagonals and the sides are 45°, and the two diagonals are equal (about 7.1 cm for a 5 cm square).

concepts.concept_name: Math Talk (section 8.5): general laws

content.text:
Math Talk (section 8.5): general laws: What general laws did you observe with respect to the angles and sides of a rectangle and its diagonals? Try to frame them.
1. Look at your table of sides and the eight angles for several rectangles.
2. Notice which numbers repeat in each row.
3. Write each repeated pattern as a rule.
4. Check the special case of a square separately.
Answer: In every rectangle: opposite sides are equal and all angles are 90°; the two diagonals are equal in length (and cut each other into equal halves); each diagonal divides the opposite angles into two angles that add up to 90°; the angles the diagonals make with the sides are equal in pairs (d = e = a = h and c = f = g = b). If the adjacent sides are equal (a square), each diagonal divides the opposite angles into 45° and 45°; if not, the two parts are unequal.

concepts.concept_name: Math Talk (section 8.5): will the laws always be true

content.text:
Math Talk (section 8.5): will the laws always be true: How can one be sure that the laws you have observed will always be true?
1. Try many different rectangles and see if the law holds each time.
2. Notice that measurements are only close, not exact.
3. Look for a reason using properties already known, for example that opposite sides are parallel.
4. A reason that works for every rectangle makes us sure.
Answer: Measuring a few examples cannot prove a law for every rectangle, because measurements are approximate and we cannot try all rectangles. We need a reason that works for any rectangle, such as using what we know (opposite sides equal, all angles 90°, alternate angles at parallel sides) to explain why the pattern must hold.

content.text:
Worked example: Construct a rectangle in which one of the diagonals divides the opposite angles into 60° and 30°.
1. Draw AB of any length. At B draw a perpendicular line (90°).
2. At A use the protractor to draw a 60° angle with AB. Where this ray meets the perpendicular from B, mark C.
3. Through A draw a line perpendicular to AB. This is the line on which D lies, and angle A is now 60° + 30°.
4. Find D. Method 1: draw a perpendicular to BC at C, and D is where it meets the line through A. Method 2: with the compass take length BC and mark D on the line through A so that AD = BC.
5. Join CD. ABCD is the rectangle. Check: AB = CD, AD = BC and every angle is 90°.
Answer: Rectangle ABCD in which the diagonal AC makes 60° with side AB and 30° with side AD (angle A = 90° = 60° + 30°). The side lengths can be chosen freely, as only the angles are given.

content.text:

4. Check with a protractor: the other angle measures 30°.

concepts.concept_name: Construct Q1 (section 8.5)

content.text:
Construct Q1 (section 8.5): Construct a rectangle in which one of the diagonals divides the opposite angles into 50° and 40°.
1. Draw AB of any length. At B draw a perpendicular (90°).
2. At A draw a 50° angle with AB. The ray meets the perpendicular from B at C.
3. Draw the perpendicular to AB at A. Then the other angle at A is 90° − 50° = 40°.
4. Draw a perpendicular to BC at C. It meets the line through A at D.
5. Check: AB = CD, AD = BC, all angles 90°.
Answer: Rectangle ABCD in which the diagonal AC makes 50° with side AB and 40° with side AD (at C the diagonal makes 50° with CD and 40° with CB). Side lengths are free.

concepts.concept_name: Construct Q2 (section 8.5)

content.text:
Construct Q2 (section 8.5): Construct a rectangle in which one of the diagonals divides the opposite angles into 45° and 45°. What do you observe about the sides? a) Construct the rectangle. b) What do you observe about the sides?
1. Draw AB of any length. At B draw a perpendicular.
2. At A draw a 45° angle with AB. It meets the perpendicular at C.
3. Draw the perpendicular to AB at A (the other angle at A is 90° − 45° = 45°).
4. Draw the perpendicular to BC at C. It meets the line through A at D.
5. Measure the sides: AB = BC = CD = DA. It is a square.
Answer: a) the rectangle is built with 45° at A next to AB and 45° next to AD; b) all the sides are equal, so it is a square.

media.description: The same order of drawing is used again, this time for a rectangle whose diagonal divides the opposite angles into fifty degrees and forty degrees. The other part of the corner comes from ninety take away fifty.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: draw the side, then the given angle at the end where the diagonal starts, and let the perpendiculars finish the rectangle. The second part of the corner is ninety take away the first.

media.description: A rectangle is built so that its diagonal divides the opposite angles into forty five degrees and forty five degrees, and then the sides are measured. All four sides turn out to be equal, so the rectangle is a square.

concepts.concept_name: A rectangle with a side of 5 cm and a diagonal of 7 cm

content.text:
2. Construct a rectangle where one of its sides is 5 cm and the length of a diagonal is 7 cm.
Solution
Let us draw a rough diagram.
Let us decide the steps of construction. Which line can be drawn first?
STEP 1
The base CD measuring length 5 cm can be easily constructed.
Next?
STEP 2
Draw a perpendicular to line DC at the point C. Let us call this line l.
This is easy as we know that this line is perpendicular to the base. The point B should be somewhere on this line l.
How do we spot it? What else do we know about the position of B?
We know that it is at a distance of 7 cm from the point D.

content.text:
Worked example: Construct a rectangle where one of its sides is 5 cm and the length of a diagonal is 7 cm.
1. Draw base DC = 5 cm.
2. At C draw a line l perpendicular to DC (90°).
3. With the compass opened to 7 cm and centre D, draw an arc that cuts line l. The cutting point is B (DB = 7 cm).
4. Draw a perpendicular to DC at D and a perpendicular to BC at B. They meet at A. (Or mark A with the compass so that DA = CB and AB = DC.)
5. Check: AB = 5 cm, BC = AD, angles 90°, diagonal DB = 7 cm.
Answer: Rectangle ABCD with DC = AB = 5 cm and diagonal DB = 7 cm. The other two sides AD = BC come out about 4.9 cm and all four angles are 90°.

Worked example: To construct the rectangle with a side of 5 cm and a diagonal of 7 cm, which line can be drawn first?
1. Only one length that is a side is known: 5 cm.
2. Draw this side first as the base CD.
3. The other points can be found from it.
Answer: The base CD, which is 5 cm long.

concepts.concept_name: A circle holds every point at 7 cm from D

content.text:
One of the ways of marking B is by taking a ruler and trying to move it around to get a point on line l that is 7 cm from point D. However, this requires trial and error. There is another efficient method which doesn't involve trial and error.
For this, instead of trying to get that one required point of distance 7 cm from D, let us explore a way of getting all the points of distance 7 cm from D.
We know what this shape is!
STEP 3
Method 1
Construct a circle of radius 7 cm with point D as the centre.
Can you spot the point B here? Remember that it is 7 cm away from point D and on the line l.
Consider the point at which the circle and the line intersect. What is its distance from point D? If needed, check your figure. What do you observe?
The point where the circle intersects the line l is the required point B.
Method 2
To locate the point B, was it necessary to draw the entire circle? We can see that only the arc near the line l is needed. So, the third step can also be done as shown in the figure below.

1. The diagonal DB = 7 cm.
2. So B is 7 cm from D.
3. B is also on line l.
4. B is the point of l that is 7 cm from D.
Answer: B is at a distance of 7 cm from the point D (since the diagonal DB is 7 cm).

concepts.concept_name: A circle holds every point at 7 cm from D

content.text:
Worked example: A circle of radius 7 cm is drawn with centre D, and it meets line l at a point. What is the distance of that point from D?
1. Every point of a circle is at the radius distance from the centre.
2. The radius is 7 cm.
3. So the point where the circle meets l is 7 cm from D, and it is B.
Answer: 7 cm. This point is the required point B.

Having marked the three points of the rectangle, we only need to complete it. Recall that we were in a similar situation in the previous problem also. We saw two methods of completing the rectangle from here. We could follow any one of those methods.
STEP 4
Construct perpendiculars to DC and BC passing through D and B, respectively. The point where these lines intersect is the fourth point A.
Check if ABCD is indeed a rectangle satisfying properties R1 and R2.

content.text:
Worked example: In the finished rectangle ABCD (DC = 5 cm, diagonal DB = 7 cm), check that it satisfies R1 (opposite sides are equal in length) and R2 (all the angles are 90°).
1. Measure AB and DC with a ruler: both 5 cm.
2. Measure AD and BC: both about 4.9 cm.
3. Check each corner with a set square or protractor: 90°.
4. So R1 and R2 hold.
Answer: Yes. AB = DC = 5 cm and AD = BC (about 4.9 cm each), and all four angles are 90°.

concepts.concept_name: Construct Q3 (section 8.5)

content.text:
Construct Q3 (section 8.5): Construct a rectangle one of whose sides is 4 cm and the diagonal is of length 8 cm.
1. Draw PQ = 4 cm.
2. At P draw a perpendicular line.
3. With the compass opened to 8 cm and centre Q, draw an arc cutting this perpendicular at S (QS = 8 cm).
4. Draw a perpendicular to PQ at Q and a line through S parallel to PQ (perpendicular to PS). They meet at R.
5. Check: PQ = SR = 4 cm, PS = QR, angles 90°, diagonal QS = 8 cm.
Answer: Rectangle PQRS with PQ = SR = 4 cm and diagonal QS = 8 cm. The other sides PS = QR are about 6.9 cm.

content.text:
STEP 1
Can you complete the figure? Try!
We need to locate the point A that is of distance 5 cm from the points B and C. You might have realised that this can be done using a ruler. However, this leads to a lot of trial and error. This construction can be further simplified. How?
If you have guessed that this can be done by the use of compass, you are right! Go ahead and explore how the point A can be located without trial and error.
There is a similarity between the problem of finding point A in this problem and point B at step 3 of the second solved example of the previous section (see page 209).
STEP 2
Draw a curve that has all its points of 5 cm from the point B; the circle centred at B should be with 5 cm radius.
Does this help in spotting the point A? Construct and explore in the figure.
The point A can be located by finding the correct point on the circle that is of distance 5 cm from the point C. Again, this can be done using a ruler. But can we use a compass for this?
STEP 3
Method 1
Take a radius of 5 cm in the compass and with C as the centre, draw a circle.
Are you able to spot the point A? Check the figure in your notebook. What do you observe?
See the point at which both the circles intersect. How far is it from the point B?
How far is it from C?
Thus, this is the point A!
Think
Was it necessary to draw two full circles to get the point A? We only needed part of both the circles.
Method 2

3. They meet at A, which is 5 cm from B and 5 cm from C.
4. Two short arcs that cross are enough, no full circles needed.

content.text:
Worked example: The two circles of radius 5 cm centred at B and at C meet at a point (the apex A). How far is that point from B? How far is it from C? a) Distance from B b) Distance from C
1. The point lies on the circle centred at B with radius 5 cm.
2. So it is 5 cm from B.
3. It also lies on the circle centred at C with radius 5 cm, so it is 5 cm from C.
4. This is the apex A.
Answer: a) 5 cm, b) 5 cm. So it is the point A.

concepts.concept_name: Where two circles meet

content.text:
Worked example: Was it necessary to draw two full circles to get the point A?
1. The point A is where the two circles cross.
2. Only the small parts near the crossing matter.
3. Draw just arcs from B and from C with 5 cm radius.
4. Where they cross is A.
Answer: No. Only a part of each circle is needed, so short arcs of radius 5 cm from B and from C that cross at A are enough.

concepts.concept_name: Building the house

content.text:
House
Recreate this figure.
Note that all the lines forming the border of the house are of length 5 cm.
Solution
The first task is to identify in what sequence the lines and curve will have to be drawn.
So the point A could have been obtained just by drawing arcs of radius 5 cm from points B and C.
Join A to B and A to C by straight lines.
Having obtained point A, what remains is the construction of the remaining arc. How do we do it?
Can we use the fact that A is of distance 5 cm from both B and C?
STEP 4
Take 5 cm radius in the compass and from A, draw the arc touching B and C as shown in the figure.
The house is ready!

content.text:
Worked example: Recreate this house figure. All the lines forming the border of the house are of length 5 cm. The house has a rectangular part with base DE = 5 cm and vertical sides DB = 5 cm and EC = 5 cm, a door 1 cm wide and 2 cm tall on the base, a roof with sides AB = 5 cm and AC = 5 cm meeting at the top point A, and a curved arc from B to C.
1. Draw base DE = 5 cm. Draw perpendiculars at D and E and mark B and C each 5 cm up. Draw the door, 1 cm wide and 2 cm tall, on DE.
2. To find A, which is 5 cm from both B and C: set the compass to 5 cm and draw an arc from B (the circle of all points 5 cm from B).
3. With the same 5 cm opening draw an arc from C. The two arcs meet at A, which is 5 cm from B and 5 cm from C. Join AB and AC.
4. With the compass at A and radius 5 cm, draw the arc from B to C (it bulges down into the house).
5. Check AB = AC = 5 cm.
Answer: A house with DE = DB = EC = AB = AC = 5 cm, a door 1 cm wide and 2 cm tall on the base, apex A found as the point 5 cm from both B and C, and an arc from B to C drawn with centre A and radius 5 cm. Since BC = 5 cm as well, triangle ABC has all sides 5 cm.

tool_config.title: Equal Distance Explorer
tool_config.idea: A point at a given distance from each of two points lies where an arc around the first meets an arc around the second; the arcs meet only if the radius is big enough.
tool_config.screen: Two points B and C with a distance slider; a radius dial; arcs drawn around B and C that sweep out; the crossing point marked with its distance from B and from C.
student_does: Predict whether the arcs will cross before setting the radius.
Set the distance between B and C and the radius.
Read the crossing point and its distance, or say that there is none.
challenges: B and C are 5 cm apart, radius 5 cm: distance of the crossing point from B? (5 cm)
B and C are 6 cm apart, radius 5 cm: how high above the middle of BC is the crossing point? (4 cm)
B and C are 8 cm apart, radius 5 cm: how high above the middle? (3 cm)
B and C are 8 cm apart, radius 3 cm: do the arcs cross? (no)
B and C are 10 cm apart, radius 5 cm: where do the arcs meet? (at the middle of BC)
B and C are 5 cm apart, radius 5 cm: how high is the crossing point above BC, to the nearest tenth? (4.3 cm)
feedback: Drawing only one arc leaves many possible points; the tool shows the second arc cutting it at the point.
A radius that is too small leaves a gap between the arcs, and the tool shows it.
A solved card shows both arcs and the crossing point with its two distances.

concepts.concept_name: Construct Q1 (section 8.6)

content.text:
Construct Q1 (section 8.6): Construct a bigger house in which all the sides are of length 7 cm.
1. Draw DE = 7 cm, then perpendiculars at D and E; mark B and C 7 cm above D and E.
2. Draw a door on DE (the book's solution uses 2 cm wide and 3 cm tall).
3. With the compass at 7 cm, draw arcs from B and from C. They meet at A. Join AB and AC.
4. With the compass at A and radius 7 cm, draw the arc from B to C.
5. Check: every border line is 7 cm.
Answer: A house like the earlier one with all border lines 7 cm: DE = DB = EC = AB = AC = 7 cm, apex A 7 cm from B and from C, and an arc BC with centre A and radius 7 cm. The book's solution draws a door 2 cm wide and 3 cm tall.

content.text:
Construct Q2 (section 8.6): Try to recreate ‘A Person’, ‘Wavy Wave’, and ‘Eyes’ from the section ‘Artwork’, using ideas involved in the ‘House’ construction.
1. Person: draw a circle with the compass for the head, then a neck line and a square for the body.
2. Wave: mark equal parts on a central line and draw half circles with the compass, one above and the next below.
3. Eyes: draw a light horizontal line. From a point A above it draw the lower curve, and from a point B below it draw the upper curve, with the same compass opening, so the two arcs meet at the ends.
4. Place A and B symmetrically (same distance from the line) so the eye is symmetrical.
5. Copy the eye for the second one and add the pupils.
Answer: Open drawing. A correct drawing shows: A Person (a circle for the head, for example radius 2 cm, a short neck line, and a 4 cm by 4 cm square body in the book's solution); Wavy Wave (equal half circles drawn alternately above and below a central line); Eyes (two matching lens-shaped eyes, each made from an upper and a lower arc drawn from compass points A above and B below, placed symmetrically, with a filled round pupil).

concepts.concept_name: Construct Q3 (section 8.6)

content.text:
Construct Q3 (section 8.6): Is there a 4-sided figure in which all the sides are equal in length but is not a square? If such a figure exists, can you construct it? a) Does such a figure exist? b) Can you construct it?
1. Take side length 5 cm. Draw AB = 5 cm and AC = 5 cm with angle A not equal to 90°, for example 60°.
2. The fourth point D must be 5 cm from both B and C.
3. With the compass at 5 cm, draw an arc from B and an arc from C. They cross at D.
4. Join BD and CD. All four sides AB, AC, BD, CD are 5 cm.
5. The angles are not 90°, so it is not a square.
Answer: a) Yes, a rhombus (diamond) with four equal sides and angles that are not 90°; b) yes, it can be constructed with compass arcs.

concepts.concept_name: What we found about constructions

content.text:
Let's Summarise!
All the points of a circle are at the same distance from its centre. This distance is called the radius of the circle.
A compass can be used to construct circles and their parts.
A rough diagram can be useful in planning how to construct a given figure.
A rectangle can be constructed given the lengths of its sides or that of one of its sides and a diagonal.
