learning_objectives.objective_text: Students restate that a circle is all points at one distance from its centre, how a rough diagram plans a construction, and how a rectangle is built from sides or from a side and a diagonal.

objectives.objective_text: Students describe how the circles in each artwork picture touch, overlap or share a centre, and say why freehand circles come out uneven.
Students mark points that are 4 cm from a point P with a ruler in many directions and say that together they form a circle with centre P.
Students open a compass to 4 cm against a ruler, draw the circle with the tip fixed at the centre, and state that every point on it is one radius from the centre.
Students set a radius on the compass tool, fix the centre, draw circles that touch, overlap or share a centre, and check points on them with a ruler.
Students find the radius and the compass tip position for a half circle drawn on a segment, and draw two equal half circles on the two halves of a line, one above and one below.
Students choose a central line length on the wave tool, set the radius for each half circle, and draw waves that alternate above and below the line.
Students draw a circle for a head and an arc for the curved top of a body by trying tip positions above the body until the arc passes through both top corners.
Students draw an almond-shaped eye from an upper and a lower arc of the same radius, with the two compass tips the same distance from the middle line, and fill the pupil.
Students draw two identical arcs, smaller than a half circle, one above and one below a central line, as in the neck of A Person.
Students state R1 and R2 for a rectangle and S1 and S2 for a square, and decide from sides and angles whether a figure is a rectangle, a square or neither.
Students list the valid names of a square or rectangle by travelling round the corners in order, and say why a name that jumps across the figure is not valid.
Students measure sides and angles on the checker tool and classify each figure as a square, a rectangle, a rhombus or none of these.
Students check the two square properties for a turned square and explain that rotation keeps lengths and angles, so the shape does not change.
Students move across and down by dot counts to show that two sides are equal and meet at 90°, without any measuring instrument.
Students draw a rectangle with four equal squares near its corners, and tilted squares and rectangles, on dot paper by counting dots, then check their properties.
Students construct a square PQRS of side 6 cm by drawing PQ, two perpendiculars and two equal lengths, and check its sides and angles.
Students use the square's properties to explain why PS must be 6 cm and why RS, the angle at R and the angle at S are fixed once PQ and two perpendiculars are drawn.
Students carry out each step of a square or rectangle construction on the stepper tool, choosing the ruler, protractor or compass action, and check the finished figure.
Students explain why a four-sided figure with all angles 90° cannot have unequal opposite sides, by using the equal distance between two perpendiculars.
Students construct rectangles of 4 cm by 6 cm and 2 cm by 10 cm with a ruler and a set square or compass, and check both rectangle properties.
Students construct a rectangle with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm, place X on AD and Y on BC, and predict where X and Y are closest and where they are farthest.
Students measure XY for chosen positions of X and Y and record each case as a row of a table with the distance of X from A, the distance of Y from B and the length XY.
Students show that equal distances of X from A and of Y from B give XY equal to AB and ABYX a rectangle, and that the farthest XY is a diagonal of the rectangle.
Students drag X and Y along two opposite sides of a rectangle on the tool, read the length XY, and find the nearest and the farthest positions for different rectangles.
Students draw a rough diagram of a rectangle ACDF made of squares ABEF and BCDE, name the equal sides, and construct it for AF = 4 cm.
Students construct a rectangle that divides into three identical squares by repeating one compass length along a line, and give its sides.
Students give sides of a rectangle that cannot be split into two identical squares and of one that cannot be split into three, using the length-to-breadth test.
Students construct an 8 cm by 4 cm rectangle with a square drawn inside it that shares its centre, using a rough diagram to find the side and the gaps.
Students locate the centre of a square as the meeting point of its two diagonals and use it as the compass tip for a circular hole in the middle.
Students plan and construct a staircase, a shading, a hole and a curve built from squares, circles and arcs, using a rough diagram to choose lengths and tip positions.
Students predict, construct and measure to show that the two diagonals of a rectangle are equal in length.
Students measure the two angles a diagonal makes at a corner, show that they add up to 90°, and name the pairs of equal angles formed by both diagonals.
Students change the sides of a rectangle on the tool, read both diagonals and the angles they make with the sides, and describe what stays the same.
Students explain that the diagonal splits a corner into equal parts only when two adjacent sides are equal, so the rectangle is a square.
Students show that in a square the two diagonals are equal and all eight angles formed with the sides are 45°.
Students state the laws of sides, angles and diagonals of a rectangle and explain why measuring a few rectangles cannot prove a law for all rectangles.
Students construct a rectangle ABCD in which the diagonal AC splits the corner A into 60° and 30°, using the fact that the two angles add up to 90°.
Students construct rectangles whose diagonal splits a corner into 50° and 40°, and into 45° and 45°, and say what the second one shows about the sides.
Students plan the order of steps for a rectangle with a side of 5 cm and a diagonal of 7 cm, and decide which line to draw first.
Students use a circle or an arc of radius 7 cm centred at D to find the point B on the line l, and explain why only a short arc is needed.
Students complete the rectangle with perpendiculars at D and B, and check that opposite sides are equal and every angle is 90°.
Students build a rectangle from a side and a diagonal on the tool, and read the second side that comes out.
Students show that a point where two circles of radius 5 cm meet is 5 cm from both centres, and say why short arcs are enough.
Students construct the house with sides of 5 cm, finding the apex with two arcs and drawing the curved top from the apex.
Students place two points on the tool, set a radius, and watch where the two arcs cross to locate the point at that distance from both, then build a bigger house.
Students construct a four-sided figure with all sides 5 cm and an angle other than 90°, by finding the fourth corner with two arcs.
Students decide whether an equal-sided figure must be a square, construct one that is not, and recreate the Person, Wavy Wave and Eyes artwork with arcs.
Students restate that a circle is all points at one distance from its centre, how a rough diagram plans a construction, and how a rectangle is built from sides or from a side and a diagonal.

video_coverage.book_item: Book item: Look at five artwork pictures: two circles of the same size side by side and touching; two circles one inside the other with the same centre (the inner one about half the size of the outer); three equal circles in a row, each overlapping the next; a mouse face (one big circle for the face, two smaller circles for the ears, two small circles with dots for the eyes, a dot for the nose and a short line for the mouth); and two lines crossing like an X with a small circle at the bottom end of each line. Try drawing them freehand.
Book item: Mark a point P in your notebook. Then mark as many points as possible, in different directions, that are 4 cm away from P.
Book item: Imagine marking all the points that are 4 cm away from the point P. How would they look?
Book item: How can a compass be used to mark points that are 4 cm from P?
Book item: Take a point on the circle drawn with centre P and radius 4 cm. Is its distance from P equal to 4 cm, less than 4 cm or greater than 4 cm? What about any other point on the circle?

Book item: Using a ruler and a compass, recreate the artwork pictures: two touching circles, two circles with the same centre, three overlapping circles, the mouse face, and the X with two small circles. Try to make them look as good as the book's pictures.

Book item: Construct this wave: a central straight line AB = 8 cm. The first wave is a half circle on the left half of AB lying above the line (A to X), and the second wave is a half circle on the right half lying below the line (X to B). Both half circles are shaded with vertical lines.

Book item: In the wave with a central line AB = 8 cm, the first wave is a half circle from A to X on the line AB. What radius should be taken in the compass to get this half circle? What should be the length of AX? a) What radius should be taken in the compass? b) What should be the length of AX?
Book item: Take a central line of a different length and try to draw the wave on it.

Book item: Draw a person made of a circle for the head, a short straight neck line below it, and a body that is a rectangle whose top edge is a curved arc dipping in the middle. How will you draw the curved top of the body with a compass? Where should the tip be placed and what radius should be used?

Book item: How do you draw these eyes with a compass? Each eye is an almond shape made of an upper curve and a lower curve meeting at two pointed corners, with a filled dark circle (pupil) in the middle. The two eyes sit side by side and are identical.

Book item: Try to recreate the figure where the waves are smaller than a half circle (as appearing in the neck of the figure 'A Person'). The challenge here is to get both the waves to be identical. This may be tricky!
Book item: What shapes are a rectangle and four small squares drawn in a group? What makes them squares and rectangles?

Book item: A rectangle ABCD has corners A (top left), B (top right), C (bottom right), D (bottom left). Besides ABCD it can be named BCDA, CDAB, DABC, ADCB, DCBA, CBAD and BADC. Can a rectangle be named using any combination of the labels around its corners? What names are allowed and what names are not?

Book item: Which of the following is not a name for this square? The square has corners S (top left), P (top right), Q (bottom right) and R (bottom left). 1. PQSR 2. SPQR 3. RSPQ 4. QRSP 1) PQSR 2) SPQR 3) RSPQ 4) QRSP

Book item: Identify if there are any squares in this collection. Use measurements if needed. On a dot grid there are four tilted 4-sided figures with corners on dots: A is a diamond whose left to right span equals its top to bottom span (about 8 dots each way); B is a diamond about 6 dots wide and 8 dots tall; C is a diamond about 10 dots wide and 8 dots tall; D is a small tilted long rectangle.

Book item: A square piece of paper has all its sides equal and all angles 90°. It is rotated (tilted so it looks like a diamond). Is it still a square? Are all the sides still equal? Are all the angles still 90°?

Book item: Is it possible to reason out if the sides are equal or not, and if the angles are right or not, without using any measuring instruments in the above figure? Can we do this by only looking at the position of corners in the dot grid?

Book item: Draw the rectangle and four squares configuration (a rectangle in the middle, about twice as wide as tall, with four equal small squares placed near its four corners, one outside each corner, not touching it) on a dot paper. What did you do to recreate this figure so that the four squares are placed symmetrically around the rectangle? Discuss with your classmates.

Book item: Draw at least 3 rotated squares and rectangles on a dot grid. Draw them such that their corners are on the dots. Verify if the squares and rectangles that you have drawn satisfy their respective properties.
Book item: How would you construct a square with a side of 6 cm? A square PQRS of side length 6 cm is constructed.
Book item: In the construction of square PQRS with PQ = 6 cm, can you see why PS should be 6 cm long?
Book item: In the square PQRS of side 6 cm just constructed, how long is the side RS and what are the measures of ∠R and ∠S?
Book item: Is it possible to construct a 4-sided figure in which all the angles are equal to 90° but opposite sides are not equal?
Book item: Draw a rectangle with sides of length 4 cm and 6 cm. After drawing, check if it satisfies both the rectangle properties.
Book item: Draw a rectangle of sides 2 cm and 10 cm. After drawing, check if it satisfies both the rectangle properties.
Book item: Construct a rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm.

Book item: In rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm, X moves along side AD and Y moves along side BC. At which positions will the points X and Y be at their closest? When do you think they will be the farthest? What does your intuition say? Discuss with your classmates.
Book item: How does the minimum distance between the points X and Y compare to the length of AB (7 cm)?

Book item: Rectangle ABCD has AB = 7 cm, BC = 4 cm. Measure XY and fill in: When X is 5 mm away from A and Y is 3 cm away from B, XY = __ cm __ mm. When X is 1 cm away from A and Y is 1 cm away from B, XY = __ cm __ mm. When X is 2 cm away from A and Y is 4 cm away from B, XY = __ cm __ mm. a) X is 5 mm from A and Y is 3 cm from B b) X is 1 cm from A and Y is 1 cm from B c) X is 2 cm from A and Y is 4 cm from B

Book item: Is there a shorthand way of writing it down? In all the sentences, only the position of X, Y and the length XY changes. So we could write this as a table with columns: Distance of X from A, Distance of Y from B, Length of XY. Fill the table for the three cases above. 1) X from A: 5 mm, Y from B: 3 cm 2) X from A: 1 cm, Y from B: 1 cm 3) X from A: 2 cm, Y from B: 4 cm

Book item: What happens to the length XY when X and Y are placed at the same distance away from A and B, respectively? Fill the table: X from A is 5 mm and Y from B is 5 mm; X from A is 1 cm and Y from B is 1 cm; X from A is 1 cm 5 mm and Y from B is 1 cm 5 mm. 1) 5 mm and 5 mm 2) 1 cm and 1 cm 3) 1 cm 5 mm and 1 cm 5 mm

Book item: In each of these cases (X and Y at the same distance from A and B), observe 1. how the length XY compares to that of AB and 2. the shape of the 4-sided figure ABYX. 1) How XY compares with AB 2) Shape of ABYX
Book item: How does the farthest distance between X and Y compare with the length of AC? BD? (AC and BD are the diagonals of rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm.)
Book item: Construct a rectangle ACDF that can be divided into two identical squares ABEF and BCDE, with no measurements imposed. If AF is assigned 4 cm, what must the length of AC be?
Book item: Construct a rectangle that can be divided into 3 identical squares (a rectangle split by two vertical lines into three equal squares).

Book item: Give the lengths of the sides of a rectangle that cannot be divided into two identical squares, and of a rectangle that cannot be divided into three identical squares. a) Cannot be divided into two identical squares b) Cannot be divided into three identical squares

Book item: Construct a rectangle of sides 8 cm and 4 cm. How will you construct a square inside, as shown in the figure, such that the centre of the square is the same as the centre of the rectangle? (The square touches the top and bottom of the rectangle and sits in the middle of its length.)
Book item: Construct a square with a circular hole whose centre is the same as the centre of the square.

Book item: Construct three squares of side 4 cm placed in a staircase, each touching the next at one corner (the top right corner of a lower square touches the bottom left corner of the square above it). Now try with squares of side 7 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm placed in the same way, with the 7 cm square at the bottom left and the 3 cm square at the top right.

Book item: Construct the figure: a large square divided into smaller squares, some halved by diagonals with one half shaded with parallel lines, and a plain larger square in a corner. Choose measurements of your choice. The larger 4-sided figure is a square and so are the smaller ones.
Book item: Construct a large square divided into 4 equal smaller squares (2 by 2) with a circular hole in the centre of each small square.

Book item: This is a square with 8 cm sidelengths. Construct it so that four arcs, one on each side, bulge uniformly inwards from each side, each arc going from one corner of its side to the other corner.

Book item: Rectangle PQRS has diagonals PR and QS. Predict whether the two diagonals are equal in length, then construct a rectangle (for example 6 cm by 4 cm) and measure both diagonals. What do you find?

Book item: In rectangle PQRS the diagonal PR divides angle R into g and h, and divides angle P into c and d. Predict, then measure: are g and h equal? Are c and d equal? a) Are g and h equal? b) Are c and d equal?

Book item: In rectangle PQRS, with both diagonals drawn, the eight angles formed by the diagonals and the sides are a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h (at P: c and d; at Q: e and f; at R: g and h; at S: a and b; c is next to side PS, d next to PQ, e next to QP, f next to QR, g next to RQ, h next to RS, a next to SR, b next to SP). Measure them. Which angles are equal?
Book item: How should the rectangle be constructed so that the diagonal divides the opposite angles into equal parts?

Book item: In your experiment, consider the case when all four sides of the rectangle are equal, that is, a square. Draw a square (for example with side 5 cm), draw both diagonals, and see what happens.
Book item: What general laws did you observe with respect to the angles and sides of a rectangle and its diagonals? Try to frame them.
Book item: How can one be sure that the laws you have observed will always be true?
Book item: Construct a rectangle in which one of the diagonals divides the opposite angles into 60° and 30°.
Book item: Angle A of the rectangle is divided by the diagonal into two angles. One measures 60°. Check what the other angle is.
Book item: Construct a rectangle in which one of the diagonals divides the opposite angles into 50° and 40°.

Book item: Construct a rectangle in which one of the diagonals divides the opposite angles into 45° and 45°. What do you observe about the sides? a) Construct the rectangle. b) What do you observe about the sides?
Book item: Construct a rectangle where one of its sides is 5 cm and the length of a diagonal is 7 cm.
Book item: To construct the rectangle with a side of 5 cm and a diagonal of 7 cm, which line can be drawn first?
Book item: Line l is perpendicular to DC at C, and the point B must lie on l. What else do we know about the position of B?
Book item: A circle of radius 7 cm is drawn with centre D, and it meets line l at a point. What is the distance of that point from D?
Book item: In the finished rectangle ABCD (DC = 5 cm, diagonal DB = 7 cm), check that it satisfies R1 (opposite sides are equal in length) and R2 (all the angles are 90°).
Book item: Construct a rectangle one of whose sides is 4 cm and the diagonal is of length 8 cm.
Book item: Construct a rectangle one of whose sides is 3 cm and the diagonal is of length 7 cm.
Book item: The two circles of radius 5 cm centred at B and at C meet at a point (the apex A). How far is that point from B? How far is it from C? a) Distance from B b) Distance from C
Book item: Was it necessary to draw two full circles to get the point A?

Book item: Recreate this house figure. All the lines forming the border of the house are of length 5 cm. The house has a rectangular part with base DE = 5 cm and vertical sides DB = 5 cm and EC = 5 cm, a door 1 cm wide and 2 cm tall on the base, a roof with sides AB = 5 cm and AC = 5 cm meeting at the top point A, and a curved arc from B to C.
Book item: Construct a bigger house in which all the sides are of length 7 cm.
Book item: Try to recreate ‘A Person’, ‘Wavy Wave’, and ‘Eyes’ from the section ‘Artwork’, using ideas involved in the ‘House’ construction.

Book item: Is there a 4-sided figure in which all the sides are equal in length but is not a square? If such a figure exists, can you construct it? a) Does such a figure exist? b) Can you construct it?
